claims.text: The 2009 keynote's table of order-of-magnitude latencies gives a first-level cache reference at about 0.5 nanoseconds, a main memory reference at about 100, sending 2 kilobytes over a gigabit network at about 20,000, a round trip within the same datacenter at about 500,000, a disk seek at about 10,000,000, and reading 1 megabyte sequentially from disk at about 30,000,000.

source.title: Jeffrey Dean, Large-Scale Distributed Systems at Google: Current Systems and Future Directions, keynote at LADIS 2009, October 2009 — the slide deck carrying Numbers Everyone Should Know

claims.text: A correction to the way these figures are usually taught. They are stale, and predictably so: an interactive update exists precisely because someone noticed a real-world latency number was an order of magnitude smaller than the memorised figure, hardware performance increasing exponentially. There is also a plausible claim that the table's provenance predates that keynote.

source.title: Colin Scott, Latency Numbers Every Programmer Should Know — an interactive update of the 2009 figures, motivated by hardware performance increasing exponentially

claims.text: The queuing relationship L equals lambda times W — items in the system equals arrival rate times time in system — holds independently of the arrival distribution, the service distribution and the service order, which makes it usable in an estimate without knowing any of them.

source.title: John D. C. Little, A Proof for the Queuing Formula: L = lambda W, Operations Research 9(3):383-387, June 1961, doi 10.1287/opre.9.3.383

beats.broke: you have to choose between designs before either exists, and the choice turns on quantities nobody has measured because the thing has not been built
beats.fix: estimate to an order of magnitude using a handful of remembered ratios and arithmetic you can do aloud, because the decision usually turns on whether a number is thousands or billions rather than on its exact value
beats.cost: the remembered figures go stale at different rates, so the method outlives the constants and anyone who memorised the constants without the method will be confidently wrong
beats.interview: how you would estimate whether a design fits on one machine
